headline: Channel edges save the week: fluke stack the Chapel Hill drop while the upper bay stays stained
subhead: With runoff still fouling the flats, I'm working current seams off the Hook and letting the back bay's snapper blues tell me where the bunker are hiding.
body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday morning before I even loaded the boat: skip the upper bay flats, go straight to the Chapel Hill Channel edge and work it on the last two hours of the outgoing. The reasoning's simple — we've had enough runoff the last couple weeks that the flats from Keyport down through Cliffwood are holding stained, warm water, and fluke don't want any part of that when there's a cleaner alternative twenty minutes away. The channel edges push tide, tide pushes bait, and bait is exactly where you want to be putting a bucktail in mid-August.

That decision paid off. We drifted the drop from the Chapel Hill Channel out past Flynn's Knoll on the last of the outgoing into the top of the incoming, and picked at fluke the whole way — nothing epic, but a steady trickle of keepers in the 18 to 21-inch range on 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets teamed with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right on bottom in 18 to 25 feet. The fish were sitting tight to the break where the mud gives way to sand and shell, which is textbook this time of year — warm water pushes fluke up shallow to feed, then they slide back down onto that harder bottom when the sun gets high. If you're marking bait on the meter right at that transition, slow down and work it twice.

Bass are still stuck in the same holding pattern we flagged a couple weeks back — said this zone typically doesn't turn over until the water starts cooling into September, and that's exactly what's playing out. Daytime striper fishing in the bay itself has been tough. The better window is first and last light, working bunker chunks or live bunker snagged fresh off the pods around Romer Shoal and Flynn's Knoll, then fished on a fishfinder rig right on the bottom as the tide starts to move. Nothing's blitzing on top in the bay — that peanut bunker topwater craziness everybody's talking about up in Rhode Island and the Cape isn't happening here, not with our water sitting warm and the bunker schools mostly holding tight and deep rather than getting corralled and pushed up. The Rip at the Hook has given up a few better fish on the last of the ebb when there's current stacking bait against the rocks, but you need to be there right at the turn — that window is short, maybe 45 minutes, and then it goes quiet again.

Snapper blues are exactly where we said they'd be — thick as fleas in the back bay, off the Keyport docks, up in the Navesink around the Highlands bridge, and along the bulkheads in Cliffwood. That's a good long-term sign. A summer full of snappers means adult bunker schools are staying close, which usually sets up a stronger adult bluefish push as things cool off. Right now the snappers themselves are good fun on ultralight gear — small silver spoons or a sliver of peanut bunker under a bobber, and kids on the dock are having a field day. The bigger blues, the 3 to 5 pound class, are showing sporadically wherever you find bunker pods getting worked from above, mostly early morning off Romer Shoal and out toward the mouth of the Shrewsbury.

Weakfish have been a disappointment, and I'm not going to sugarcoat it. Warm, stained water is exactly the wrong recipe for weakfish, and the reports back that up — scattered short fish here and there in the Navesink on the last of the incoming, nothing worth planning a trip around. If you're set on weakfish, fish the deeper holes in the river right at first light before the sun pushes the temperature up, using a bucktail tipped with a strip of squid worked slow along bottom, but keep your expectations modest.

Porgies are around Romer Shoal and out toward the Ambrose Channel edge in decent numbers if you want steady, low-drama action — bottom rigs with clam or squid strips in 25 to 35 feet will keep a rod bent, and it's a good way to spend an afternoon with kids or when the fluke bite goes quiet on the tide change. Blackfish are still off-limits until the fall season opens, so no reason to be dropping crabs on the wrecks yet, but it's worth noting the structure out there — Romer Shoal and the rockpile off the Hook — will be worth marking once October rolls around.

Looking ahead, I don't expect a dramatic shift through the coming week. The moon's building back toward the August 28 full, and that extra tidal push should sharpen the current-driven spots — the Rip, the Chapel Hill edge, the deeper cuts off Flynn's Knoll — even if the broader pattern stays the same until real cooling starts in September. If I had one day to fish, I'd take the last two hours of an outgoing tide on the channel edge with bucktails for fluke, then swing over to Romer Shoal at last light and soak a bunker chunk for whatever bass are moving through. Keep it simple, follow the moving water, and don't waste time on the stagnant flats until the rain stops giving them a reason to be dirty.
